rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hijazi Arabic puts the exception in the accusative after a negative, construing it as a corrective ‘but’: ‘there is no one there but a donkey.’
rows.anchor: وهو لغة أهل الحجاز وذلك قولك ما فيها أحد إلا حمارا جاءوا به على معنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamim raises the exception, treating أحد as emphatic and the following noun as its replacement: ‘there is no one there but a donkey.’
rows.anchor: فيقولون لا أحد فيها إلا حمار أرادوا ليس فيها إلا حمار ولكنه ذكر أحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further construal makes the exception the place’s sole inhabitant; Abu Dhuʾayb’s poem calls the echoes of the graves his companions, and other examples identify an exception with the speaker’s defining quality.
rows.anchor: وإن شئت جعلته إنسانها قال الشاعر وهو أبو ذؤيب الهذلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the exception is a verbal noun outside the preceding category, as in ‘his authority is only affectation,’ the construction means ‘but affectation.’
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك من المصادر ماله عليه سلطان إلا التكلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 52:28 the Hijazi accusative treats following الظن as a corrective exception to there being no knowledge.
rows.anchor: ما لهم به من علم إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tamim raises this construction and treats following الظن, good opinion, or affectation as the relevant knowledge or authority.
rows.anchor: هذا كله يجعلونه اتباع الظن علمهم

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil explains the raised reading by analogy with poetry that calls a painful blow the warriors’ greeting, just as Tamim calls conjecture their knowledge.
rows.anchor: الرفع في هذا على قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception in 36:43 likewise denotes a mercy from God, not an item in the class of rescuers or cries for help.
rows.anchor: ولا هم ينقذون إلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic exceptions such as ‘no reproach but the sword’ support the analysis where the exception is identified with the preceding notion, especially when both nouns are definite.
rows.anchor: ما أتاني زيد إلا عمرو وما أعانه إخوانكم إلا إخوانه

rows.speaker: يونس عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Yunus reports Abu ʿAmr’s rule, which Sībawayh calls the analogical account: غدوة and بكرة lose tanwin when used as definite names for a time, whether established by context or stated alone.
rows.anchor: يونس عن أبي عمرو وهو قوله أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ضحوة and عشية remain indefinite in every case, like صباحا and مساء; context can nevertheless identify them as that day’s morning or evening.
rows.anchor: فأما ضحوة وعشية فلا يكونان إلا نكرة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil permits غدوة and بكرة with اليوم, treating them like ضحوة.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل أنه يجوز أن تقول

rows.speaker: أبو الخطاب
rows.claim: Abu al-Khattab heard a trusted Arab use بكرة for an arrival later the same day or the next day; Sībawayh connects this usage with 19:62.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو الخطاب أنه سمع من يوثق به من العرب يقول آتيك بكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As an adverb, سحر is indeclinable; with من or عند it takes the article, while its indefinite use is restricted to a specially shifted construction.
rows.anchor: وأما سحر إذا كان ظرفا فإن ترك

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs omit tanwin from عشية, as they do from غدوة.
rows.anchor: بعض العرب يدع فيه التنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Time nouns have diminutives such as مغيربان الشمس and عشيان; Arabs also say عشيشية for عشية, construing it through these less regular forms.
rows.anchor: فمن ذلك قول العرب في مغرب الشمس مغيربان الشمس وفي العشى آتيك عشيانا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil derives أصيلالا from أصيلان by replacing its final ن with ل; أصيلانا confirms the underlying form.
rows.anchor: سألت الخليل عن قولك آتيك أصيلالا فقال إنما هو أصيلان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh reports al-Khalil’s explanation that plurals عشيانات and مغيربانات divide the evening or sunset period into successive parts, each treated as an عشية or مغربان.
rows.anchor: عشيانات ومغيربانات فقال جعل ذلك الحين أجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ordinary diminutives are غدية from غدوة, سحير from سحر, and ضحيا from ضحى; a verse by al-Nābigha al-Jaʿdī attests ضحيا.
rows.anchor: فأما غدوة فتحقيرها عليها تقول غدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Diminutives of time words bring one time nearer another and reduce the interval; they do not mean that the time or a place itself has been made smaller.
rows.anchor: تحقيرك هذه الأشياء الحين ولكنك تريد أن تقرب حينا من حين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When these time words are used as personal names, they take the regular diminutive pattern.
rows.anchor: وجميع ذا إذا سمي به الرجل حقر على القياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Frequent words may have irregular diminutives: إنسان becomes أنيسيان, بنون becomes أبينون, and examples include لييلية and رويجل; names revert to the regular pattern.
rows.anchor: إنسان تقول أنيسيان وفي بنون أبينون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صبية and غلمة yield أصيبية and أغيلمة on a plural pattern used for فِعال and فَعيل; some Arabs instead use the regular forms صبية and غليمة.
rows.anchor: أصيبية وفي غلمة أغيلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a form with two hamzas, the hamza before the final one is replaced by ياء; this distinguishes words such as خطايا, with a weaker substituted hamza, from forms whose hamza replaces a radical, such as قضاء.
rows.anchor: ألفا وأبدلوا مكان الهمزة التي قبل الآخر ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The replacement avoids the weight of two hamzas near two alifs and distinguishes a hamza substituted for an extra letter from one replacing a root consonant.
rows.anchor: همزتان إحداهما بدل من زائدة لأنها أضعف يعني همزة خطايا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In lightened speech hamza may become the matching long vowel: alif after fatḥa, yāʾ after kasra, or wāw after ḍamma; this is learned from usage, not a rule applied to every word.
rows.anchor: تبدل مكانها الألف إذا كان ما قبلها مفتوحا والياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic necessity can extend this replacement systematically; al-Farazdaq uses an alif because the intermediate hamza pronunciation would break the meter.
rows.anchor: راحت بمسلمة البغال عشية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Huthayl forms سلت and يسال are not ordinary in the poets’ dialects, though Sībawayh was told that سلت تسال is a dialect.
rows.anchor: وبلغنا أن سلت تسال لغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms نبي and برية take hamza replacement by lexical convention, not as a general rule; some Hijazi speakers who normally articulate hamza retain it in نبي and بريئة, a rare and disfavored usage.
rows.anchor: وقالوا نبي وبرية فألزمها أهل التحقيق البدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some speakers replace an open hamza at a word boundary, as in أونت for أو أنت and أبو يوب for أبو أيوب.
rows.anchor: العرب منها من يقول في أو أنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inside a word, some speakers delete hamza in سوأة and موأله, and in حوأب say حوب; a radical hamza behaves like a root consonant.
rows.anchor: وإن كانت في كلمة واحدة نحو سوأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speakers simplify hamza in clusters of wāws, yāʾs, and kasras, as in أحلبني بلك and أرمي مك, to avoid difficult sequences.
rows.anchor: كراهية لاجتماع الواوات والياءات والكسرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some speakers delete hamza in forms such as أنا ذو نسه and يجيك ويسوك; before wāw or yāʾ they avoid ḍamma, but may retain kasra in يرم خوانه.
rows.anchor: يحذف الهمزة ويكره الضم مع الواو والياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic often omits a recoverable verb in fixed expressions: ولا زعماتك means ولا أتوهم زعماتك, with the omitted action supplied from context.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك هذا ولا زعماتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Dhu al-Rumma’s verse about Mayya’s dwellings and the rain clouds, أذكر is omitted; the prior mention of the dwellings and familiar usage let listeners supply it.
rows.anchor: لا يذكر أذكر لكثر ذلك فى كلامهم واستعمالهم إياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In common phrases such as كل شيء ولا هذا and كل شيء ولا شتيمة حر, the imperative ‘do’ is omitted because the prohibition is obvious from the wording.
rows.anchor: كل شئ ولا هذا و كل شئ ولا شتيمة حر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Tamim speakers parse كلاهما وتمرا as ‘both are mine; give me dates,’ supplying the omitted predicate and imperative, and similarly supply a predicate after كل شيء.
rows.anchor: كلاهما وتمرا كأنه قال كلاهما لى ثابتان وزدنى تمرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising الديار makes the poem a nominal identification, ‘those are Mayya’s dwellings’; the raised form states what is already in the speaker’s mind.
rows.anchor: ومن العرب من يرفع الديار كأنه يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accusative الديار instead implies an unspoken أذكر; in ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa’s line, accusative and nominative express different intended meanings.
rows.anchor: فالذى فى نفسك ما أظهرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accusatives such as خيرا and أوسع after انتهوا, وراءك, and حسبك are governed by an omitted imperative.
rows.anchor: @QB@ انتهوا خيرا لكم @QE@

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil explains انتهوا خيرا لكم as ‘stop and enter what is better for you’; the second action is understood and its verb is omitted through frequent use.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل كأنك تحمله على ذلك المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An explicit imperative can appear in a parallel construction such as انته يا فلان أمرا قاصدا; the frequent formula انتهوا خيرا لكم has conventionalized its omission.
rows.anchor: ونظير ذلك فى الكلام قوله انته يا فلان أمرا قاصدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic accusatives such as السباعا and طيبا are licensed by material made clear from the preceding clause, even though the excerpt’s explanation is cut off.
rows.anchor: على دمه ومصرعه السباعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An embedded question beginning with أ cannot be governed internally by an earlier verb; its clause remains a new sentence even when it occupies an object position.
rows.anchor: ألف الاستفهام تمنعه من ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In فلينظر أيها أزكى طعاما, as in 18:12, the embedded interrogative clause is syntactically an object of the preceding verb while retaining its independent internal syntax.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى @QB@ فلينظر أيها أزكى طعاما @QE@

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After ليت شعري, an embedded question occupies the predicate position; after عبد الله هل رأيته, the question clause similarly has the position of a raised predicate.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك ليت شعري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām of emphasis, like the interrogative alif, prevents the verb from governing the following clause and marks the knowledge as certain and the speaker’s own.
rows.anchor: هذه اللام تمنع العمل كما تمنع ألف الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With no interrogative or emphatic lām, علم governs its object directly, as in علمت زيدا خيرا منك and the cited Qur'anic examples.
rows.anchor: لأعملت علمت كما تعمل عرفت ورأيت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a regular noun precedes an embedded question, the verb can govern that noun while the question supplies its predicate or further information.
rows.anchor: قد عرفت زيدا أبو من هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites Arab usage for accusative constructions such as قد علمته أبو من هو and قد عرفتك أي رجل أنت.
rows.anchor: وقد عرفتك أى رجل أنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With verbs that do not take a direct object, as نظر or سأل عن, the name remains inside the embedded question: اذهب فسل زيد أبو من هو means ‘ask about Zayd.’
rows.anchor: فيما لا يتعدى إلى مفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conventional formulas such as سلام عليك, ويل لك, and لعنة الله على الظالمين begin independent statements whose meanings are already established, unlike an action performed by a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: فهذه الحروف كلها مبتدأة مبنى عليها ما بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One cannot freely replace a conventional expression with an unattested one such as طعاما لك or شرابا لك to mean a prayer; these formulas follow Arabic usage.
rows.anchor: لو قلت طعاما لك وشرابا لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In طوبى لهم وحسن مآب, حسن is raised, showing a raised construction for these established expressions.
rows.anchor: يدلك على رفعها رفع حسن مآوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ويل للمطففين and ويل يومئذ للمكذبين are not prayers; they pronounce doom on people who have entered ruin and deserve the statement.
rows.anchor: لا ينبغى أن تقول إنه دعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In فقولا له قولا لينا لعله يتذكر أو يخشى, the hope belongs to Moses and Aaron, while the outcome is already known beyond their own knowledge.
rows.anchor: العلم قد أتى من وراء ما يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قاتلهم الله follows ordinary human idiom, as does the Qur'an’s use of the expression.
rows.anchor: ومثله @QB@ قاتلهم الله @QE@

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ويل له ويل طويل permits ويل طويل as apposition to the first ويل.
rows.anchor: وتقول ويل له ويل طويل فإن شئت جعلته بدلا من المبتدإ الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second ويل طويل may instead be an adjective describing the first noun.
rows.anchor: صفة له وإن شئت قلت ويل لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Or the second ويل may be a separate accusative expression meaning that woe remains upon the person continually.
rows.anchor: قلت ويل لك ويلا طويلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A bare proper name can identify someone when a sensory sign reveals them; it is as if the speaker had said هذا عبد الله or ذاك عبد الله.
rows.anchor: رأيت صورة شخص فصار آية لك على معرفة الشخص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pattern فَعول can form verbal nouns, but the same surface form may instead denote an amount, result, agent, patient, or a related noun; these meanings must be learned lexically.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك توضأت وضوءا حسنا وأولعت به ولوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وقود can refer to the act of burning or to fuel; the form with fatḥa is the more common word for firewood, while قبولا is also attested.
rows.anchor: وقدت النار وقودا عاليا وقبله قبولا والوقود أكثر والوقود الحطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: شبعه and ملء can mean the amount that satisfies or fills, unlike شبعا and ملئا when they denote the acts; طعم may likewise mean flavor or the act of tasting.
rows.anchor: شبعه وهذا شبعه إنما يريد قدر ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some forms do not differ from their verbal nouns in meaning, as in رويت ريا, أصاب ريه, طعمت طعما, نهل نهلا, and أصاب نهله.
rows.anchor: تقول رويت ريا وأصاب ريه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These patterns are not fully predictable: خرص, الكيلة, قوت, and الحلب can vary in form and meaning, and الحلب may mean the milk as well as the act of milking.
rows.anchor: فهذه أشياء تجيء مختلفة ولا تطرد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مرية denotes an amount of milk rather than the act; لعنة may name the cursed person, and الخلق may mean the created thing rather than creation.
rows.anchor: وقالوا لعنة للذي يلعن واللعنة المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: كرع is the water one drinks from; ذو تدرإ means a person with means or protection, not the act of driving away, and لعنة can mean a person notorious for cursing.
rows.anchor: الماء الذي يكرع فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms on مفعول can denote a passive result: لبن حلب is milked milk, الخلق is the created thing, and ضرب الأمير is coin struck by the emir.
rows.anchor: على المفعول وذلك قولك لبن حلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some forms denote an agent: يوم غم means a cloudy day and رجل نوم a sleeping man.
rows.anchor: ويقع على الفاعل وذلك قولك يوم غم ورجل نوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: صرى describes milk that has lightly changed in the udder; معشر كرم is likewise used with the sense of approved or pleasing.
rows.anchor: كما يقولون هو رضا إنما يريدون المرضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular member of a collective can take the collective’s pattern with feminine ة, as in بيض/بيضة, جوز/جوزة, شمط/شمطة, and شيب/شيبة.
rows.anchor: كما قالوا بيض وبيضة وجوز وجوزة
